input: Research scholarships for adult returning students

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Scholarships vary enormously by degree level, field of study, and institution type — knowing what program the user is entering narrows the search dramatically.
Eligibility criteria often depend on personal profile factors like age, gender, military status, or single-parent status, which open or close specific scholarships.
Scholarships are frequently state- or country-specific, and whether the user is studying online vs. on-campus can affect which awards apply.
The urgency of the search — how soon the user needs to enroll or apply — determines which scholarship deadlines are still viable.
Knowing where the user wants the research delivered (a simple list, a spreadsheet with deadlines, a ranked shortlist) shapes what the output should look like.
The user may prioritize maximum award amount, ease of application, or likelihood of winning — without knowing this, it is hard to rank or filter results usefully.
Some users want only scholarships (gift aid), while others are open to grants, employer tuition benefits, or fellowship programs — knowing this avoids surfacing unwanted options.

gold.taskTitle: Research Scholarships for Adult Returning Students
gold.taskDescription: Find and evaluate scholarship opportunities specifically suited to adult learners returning to higher education.

questions.title: What degree level and field are you returning to study?
questions.description: Identify the specific program type (associate, bachelor's, master's, certificate) and subject area the user plans to pursue, so scholarship results are relevant to their actual enrollment.

questions.title: Which personal background factors describe you best?
questions.description: Determine whether the user has characteristics that unlock targeted scholarships — such as being a veteran, single parent, first-generation student, or belonging to a specific demographic group.

questions.title: What country and state or region are you located in?
questions.description: Establish the user's geographic location so that state-funded programs, regional foundations, and locally based awards can be included in the research.

questions.title: When do you plan to start school or submit applications?
questions.description: Pinpoint the enrollment timeline so only scholarships with upcoming, actionable deadlines are surfaced rather than ones that have already closed or are too far out.

questions.title: How do you want the final research delivered to you?
questions.description: Clarify the preferred output format — a simple bullet list, a spreadsheet tracking deadlines and amounts, or a ranked shortlist with direct application links — so the deliverable is immediately usable.

questions.title: What matters most when comparing scholarships to each other?
questions.description: Understand the user's primary ranking criterion — highest dollar amount, fewest application requirements, best odds of winning, or something else — so results can be meaningfully prioritized.

questions.title: Are you open to grants or employer tuition aid, or scholarships only?
questions.description: Determine whether the research should stay limited to traditional scholarships or can also cover federal/state grants, employer reimbursement programs, and fellowship opportunities.
